system_message:
You are generating a synthetic but clinically grounded
conversation for exactly one hospital admission.

Rules:
1. Use only facts supported by the provided admission context.
2. The discharge notes are the backbone of the hospital-course
   narrative. Use them first.
3. The ordered problem list should shape the main clinical focus.
4. Radiology, procedures, microbiology, and the previous-admission
   summary are supporting context, not a checklist.
5. Not every packet item needs to appear in the conversation.
6. Speakers must be exactly: Doctor and Patient.
7. Every conversation line must contain:
   - turn number
   - exact timestamp
   - speaker
   - text
8. Timestamps must be monotonically increasing and stay within the
   admission start and admission end times.
9. Keep the conversation medically plausible and understandable to
   a patient.
10. Use short natural exchanges, patient questions, clarifications,
    explanations, reassurance, and follow-up discussion.
11. Do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, test findings,
    or outcomes.
12. Do not mention the dataset, packet, note types, or that the
    conversation is synthetic.
13. Generate the conversation first, then write the summary strictly from the generated conversation_lines.
14. Every claim in summary.summary_paragraph and every item in summary.problems must be explicitly supported by the conversation_lines.
15. Return output that exactly matches the required JSON schema.

previous_admission_summary_used.summary_paragraph: A 50-year-old male with a history of necrotizing soft tissue infection, psoriatic arthritis, morbid obesity, and recent pulmonary embolism was admitted from a rehabilitation facility due to worsening left leg pain, redness, and drainage. He was found to have cellulitis with elevated white blood cell count and was started on intravenous vancomycin and Zosyn. The infectious process resolved with treatment, and antibiotics were discontinued after clinical improvement. He remained on heparin infusion due to subtherapeutic INR despite high-dose warfarin, with plans to continue anticoagulation at the rehabilitation facility. A new PICC line was placed during admission due to infection concerns, and a lower extremity Doppler ruled out deep vein thrombosis. He was discharged in stable condition with follow-up arranged in acute care, hematology, and infectious disease.

Secondary diabetes mellitus without mention of complication, uncontrolled
Personal history of Methicillin resistant Staphylococcus aureus
Adrenal cortical steroids causing adverse effects in therapeutic use

diuresed, with IV and PO furosemide, from an admission weight of

episdoes of hypoxemia was noted; however the patient did not

days of his admission when he was closer to his dry weight. The 
patient had a poor quality, but nevertheless essentially normal 
echocardiogram and no definitive evidence of pulmonary edema on 
any chest imaging. The patient's severe sleep apnea likely 
contributed to several episodes of hypoxemia. He was placed on 
CPAP at night with occasional supplemental O2. During the day 
shift however he was noted to fall asleep occasionally without 
the CPAP in place.

seizure activity was noted. He was somewhat somnolent, but not

anticoagulation. They recommended checking Factor II/X levels 
and wafarin levels. Factor II/X levels were depressed. A 
warfarin level was not ordered as the test is a sendout and 
would not return this hospitalization. He was restarted on 
warfarin 30mg daily while in the MICU and after 3 days of 
therapy had an INR of 7.9. This indicated that the patient was 
likely not taking 37.5mg of warfarin daily as listed in his 
preadmission medications. After resolution of his 
supratherapeutic INR he was started on 10mg of warfarin per day 
which was quickly titrated up to 20mg daily due to a falling 
INR. His INR at discharge was 4.2. He has anticoagulation follow 
up with Dr. ___, a world expert in anticoagulation. 
Warfarin was held on the day of discharge.

#AMBULATORY TACHYCARDIA/FREQUENT PREMATURE VENTRICULAR 
CONTRACTIONS:
The patient was seen by the cardiology service on ___. His 
baseline ECG shows a high frequency of PVCs, often >10 per 
minute. The patient had several telemetry episodes which 
appeared to be sustained ventricular tachycardia. The patient 
was asymptomatic during these episodes by all accounts. The 
rhythm strips were analyzed by the cardiology fellow and felt to 
be artifact. Repeated analysis of these episodes revealed 
occasional discordance between the two recorded leads, one 
exhibiting the rhythm concerning for VT and the other with NSR 
w/ PVCs. The cardiology team could not exclude an arrhythmia 
from injected toxic substance. Ambulatory tachycardia appeared 
sinus and was thought to be secondary to deconditioning. Atrial 
tachycardia remained a possibility but the episodes resolved so 
quickly an ECG could not be performed. The cardiology team 
recommended continuation of carvedilol for frequent PVCs.

#CONCERN FOR SELF HARM/BEHAVIOR ISSUES:
On ICU day #3, despite no longer needing ICU level care as 
determined by the ICU team, the patient refused to be 
transferred to the general medical floor and requested a second 
opinion. Per RN staff the patient was found with a ""cloudy"" 
syringe in his room, PICC-line cap open and a white substance at 
injection site of PICC-line. The patient denied all accusations 
and stated he was using the syringe to apply steroid cream to 
his feet, which he is incapable of reaching. The patient was 
also noted several times during his hospitalization to be 
manipulating telemetry leads and shaking the tele box. 
Psychiatry was consulted due to the concern of self-injurious 
behavior with possible factitious disorder. Of note, Psychiatry 
was consulted in ___ for similar concerns (see note in OMR). 
Their recommendations included limit setting, security search of 
patient belongings, and clear intra-team communication about his 
care plan in order to minimize the patient's ability to distort 
and manipulate team members. His PICC line was removed 
immediately in this setting. Psychiatry diagnosed the patient 
with an adjustment disorder with anxious features. The patient 
was made aware of the diagnosis and questioned its validity. He 
denied any feelings of anxiety or depression. On multiple 
occasions the patient requested to view his medical record, but 
never officially pursued the request. He constantly questioned 
the judgement of the medical staff stating his prior research, 
subscriptions to medical journals and previous advice received 
by experts. He consistently complained that PO medications do 
not work for him, despite clear diuresis with PO furosemide and 
response to corticosteroids. He refused to take warfarin in a 
crushed slurry form, which was recommended to ensure he is 
actually ingesting the medication. On the day of discharge the 
patient was very upset about the decision to be discharged. He 
demanded a second opinion regarding discharge with a mildly 
supratherapeutic INR, and he refused discharge due to his 
reported inability to climb stairs (not consistent with Physical 
Therapy documentation) and multiple social issues. See attending 
note in ___ dated ___.

#POSITIVE BLOOD CULTURE:
The patient was reported to have a positive blood culture on 
___. The culture appeared to contain multiple organisms 
including Gram positive cocci and Gram negative rods. These 
cultures were in the setting of continued vancomycin/Zosyn 
therapy for his left lower extremity cellutlitis. Given the 
polymicrobial nature of the culture and the patient's abdominal 
pain/steroid use a CT abd/pelvis was ordered to identify a 
potential source. No intrabdominal source of infection was 
revealed. The infectious disease was consulted regarding the 
lower extremity wound and positive blood culture. They 
recommended continued antibiotics, repeat cultures and removal 
of the PICC line as soon as possible. Surveillance blood 
cultures were drawn over the next two days and yielded no 
growth. The final speciation of the lone positive culture 
returned: MICROCOCCUS/STOMATOCOCCUS SPECIES, ENTEROBACTER 
SPECIES, VIRIDANS STREPTOCOCCI. The ID team felt the blood 
culture most likely represented contamination and the left lower 
extremity no longer appeared infected. Vancomycin and Zosyn were 
discontinued on ___. The patient was afebrile throughout 
his entire hospital stay. 

# LLE WOUND: 
Please see extensive history detailed in the HPI. In short, Mr. 
___ has experienced recurrent cellutlits and abscesses in his 
left lower extremity. Several of these episodes have been 
concerning for necrotizing fasciitis. He has undergone a total 
of six operations on the wound including I&Ds, debridements and 
fasciotomies. Prior to this admission he was started on 
vancomycin and Zosyn by ___ at his rehab facility after 
an evaluation at the ___ ED by the general surgery service. 
The general surgery service recommended no antibiotics. 
Vancomycin and Zosyn were continued until ___. The wound 
did not appear actively infected during his hospitalization. 
There was minor, physiologic surround erythema and healthy 
granulation tissue throughout. QD dressing changes and wound

no debridement and outpatient follow up in 4 weeks. The patient 
repeatedly requested second opinions regarding the wound, 
despite having seen multiple general surgeons in the past month. 
He would eventually like to see a plastic surgeon regarding its

# INSULIN DEPENDENT TYPE II DIABETES MELLITUS
Blood sugar control was not a major issue this hospitalization. 
The patient was maintained on Lantus ___ and a sliding scale 
insulin. He is quite proficient at managing his blood 
glucose/carb counting, and maintains a relatively healthy diet. 

# PSORIATIC ARTHRITIS
The patient complained of moderate to severe arthritic symptoms 
in his hands, knees and shoulders in the week prior to 
discharge. Communication with his outpatient rheumatologist, Dr. 
___, lead to an increase in his dexamethasone dose from 3mg

team was also consulted and restarted Imuran at 150mg daily. He

The pain service was unable to perform trigger point injections 
for his cervicogenic headaches due to current anticoagulation. 

#HYPERLIPIDEMIA
Atorvastatin was continued throughout the hospitalization. 
 
#HYPERTENSION 
Mr. ___ was normotensive to borderline hypertensive 
throughout most of his hospitalization. Lisinopril and 
carvedilol were continued at his home doses.

Eye drops continued.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hello, Mr. ___. I’m Dr. ___. You were brought in because of shortness of breath and palpitations. Can you tell me what happened?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, at rehab I started feeling dizzy, my heart was racing, and I couldn’t catch my breath. My oxygen dropped to 74% one morning. They said it might be another pulmonary embolism.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. We reviewed your CT from the ER — no new clots were found. But you’ve had PEs before, so we’re keeping a close eye on that. Your INR was 1.9, which is low, so we’ve restarted the heparin drip for now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been on warfarin — 37.5 mg daily. Why isn’t it working? I’ve read studies about warfarin resistance.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s a good question. We’re looking into that. Hematology is helping us. We checked your Factor II and X levels — they’re low, which suggests you may not have been absorbing or taking the full dose consistently.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I take it every day. Maybe the pharmacy made a mistake?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s possible, but we also saw your INR jumped to 7.9 when we restarted warfarin at 30 mg. That suggests you weren’t on that high a dose regularly. We’ve lowered it to 10 mg and are titrating up carefully.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. What about the breathing episodes? They came on fast — tachycardia, pulsatile tinnitus, oxygen dropping.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re concerned about that. The episodes didn’t show new clots on imaging. But you mentioned a 28-pound weight gain recently. That, plus your sleep apnea, could be causing flash pulmonary edema.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it’s heart failure? My echocardiogram was normal last time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The echo we did was suboptimal due to your body habitus, but no major wall motion issues were seen. LVEF was over 55%. We think fluid overload is playing a role. We’re starting IV furosemide to help you lose some fluid.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve taken oral furosemide before. It doesn’t work as well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll try IV first, then transition to a higher oral dose. We’re also restricting fluids and salt. Your weight was 386 lbs on admission — we’re aiming to get you closer to your dry weight.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your oxygen levels have been stable overnight on room air. The chest X-ray shows no pulmonary edema. Your CPAP is helping, but staff noticed you sometimes remove it when you fall asleep during the day.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I didn’t realize. I’ll be more careful. Could the hypoxia be from sleep apnea alone?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s contributing, especially with your obesity. But the sudden drops during walking suggest more than just apnea. We’re still watching closely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We did a Doppler ultrasound — no DVT in either leg. That’s good news. Your leg wound is being cared for daily. General surgery looked at it and said no further antibiotics or surgery are needed right now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: But there’s still redness. Shouldn’t we get a second opinion? Or consider a plastic surgeon for closure?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The redness is physiologic — part of healing. Granulation tissue looks healthy. We can arrange a plastic surgery consult for the future, but now isn’t the time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We got your blood culture results back. It grew several organisms — Enterobacter, viridans strep, and Micrococcus. But since only one set was positive and you’re not febrile, we think it’s contamination, likely from the PICC line.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: But I was on antibiotics. Could it be a real infection?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: ID agrees it’s likely contamination. We repeated cultures — they’re negative. We’re stopping vancomycin and Zosyn. Your wound isn’t infected, and we don’t want to promote resistance.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You had a brief episode last night — became unresponsive for about a minute while a blood gas was being drawn. You recovered quickly. ABG showed normal oxygen and pH. No seizure activity was seen.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I remember someone asking if they were drawing a blood gas. I felt strange, like I blacked out but came back fast.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Neurology reviewed it — no signs of seizure or stroke. Given your history, psychiatry evaluated you for possible factitious disorder. They diagnosed adjustment disorder with anxious features.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m not faking anything. I’m just worried and want to understand my care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We hear your concerns. But the PICC line was found with a syringe and white residue. For safety, we removed the PICC line. We’ll use peripheral access going forward.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your INR is now 3.1 on 20 mg warfarin. That’s improving. We’re keeping you on heparin until it’s consistently therapeutic.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: When can I stop the heparin?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Soon, if your INR stays stable. You have follow-up with Dr. ___, a specialist in anticoagulation, next week.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re down to 375 lbs — great progress. No more hypoxia episodes since starting diuresis. Your heart rhythm shows frequent PVCs, but cardiology says it’s likely benign. They recommend continuing carvedilol.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I still feel palpitations. Could it be VT?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Telemetry showed what looked like VT, but rhythm strips were inconsistent — likely artifact. You were asymptomatic. No evidence of toxic ingestion. We’ll keep monitoring.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your CT abdomen showed no abscess or fistula. Some gallbladder sludge, but nothing requiring action now. Renal cyst noted — likely benign.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Any link to my abdominal discomfort?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not clearly. Your symptoms don’t match. We’ll watch it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your rheumatologist increased your dexamethasone to 4.5 mg for joint pain. We also restarted azathioprine. Pain management added OxyContin 30 mg twice daily for better control.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been asking for stronger pain relief. Why did it take so long?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We needed to ensure it was safe with your anticoagulation. We avoided injections due to bleeding risk. Oral opioids are now appropriate.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your INR is 4.2 — therapeutic. We’ve held warfarin today. You’ll restart at home based on your clinic’s instructions.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So I’m going home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re planning discharge tomorrow if all goes well. You’re at 366 lbs, breathing well, and your wound is healing.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m not sure I’m ready. I can’t climb stairs. And my INR is still high.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your INR is mildly elevated but safe for discharge. Physical therapy says you’re independent with mobility. Home health will assist with wound care and monitoring.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’d like a second opinion before discharge.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I understand your concern, but your condition is stable, and further delay isn’t medically indicated. We’ve reviewed everything with the team.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good news — you’re cleared for discharge today. Your oxygen is 99% on room air, weight is stable, and INR is appropriate.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about my follow-ups?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You have appointments with anticoagulation clinic, rheumatology, general surgery for your wound, and psychiatry. We’re sending all instructions to your home team.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my medications?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll continue insulin, atorvastatin, lisinopril, carvedilol, dexamethasone, azathioprine, and now oral furosemide 80 mg twice daily. OxyContin for pain, plus Dilaudid as needed. Warfarin will restart per your clinic.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No more IV antibiotics?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Correct. Your wound is clean, and cultures suggest the positive blood culture was contamination. No need for further antibiotics.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the CPAP?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Use it every night. It’s crucial for preventing hypoxia. We’ll ensure you have it at home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I just want to stay out of the hospital.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We all do. Keep up with your follow-ups, take your meds, and call if you have chest pain, severe shortness of breath, or wound changes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: One more thing — your wound care: clean daily, use antimicrobial dressing, pack gently, cover with gauze and wrap. Home health will help.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll follow it exactly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Great. We’ll get your discharge papers ready. Take care, Mr. ___.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Doctor, before I go — can I see my medical record?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You can request it through medical records. We can’t release it at the bedside, but the team will help you with the process.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’d like to understand the adjustment disorder diagnosis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Psychiatry felt your anxiety about your health, combined with the PICC incident and telemetry manipulation, suggests adjustment difficulties. Outpatient therapy can help.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I just advocate for myself.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: And that’s important. We want you to be involved. But we also need to ensure your safety and the integrity of your care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I understand. I’ll follow up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re here to support you. Take care, and we’ll see you in clinic.

summary.summary_paragraph: A 50-year-old male with morbid obesity, steroid-dependent psoriatic arthritis, insulin-dependent diabetes, and obstructive sleep apnea was admitted from a rehabilitation facility due to recurrent episodes of hypoxemia, palpitations, and concern for pulmonary embolism. Initial evaluation ruled out new clots, but the patient had a subtherapeutic INR and a history of warfarin resistance.
